questions.question: What core theological dispute divided the Roman Catholic Jesuit missionaries from the Ethiopian Orthodox Church (EOC)?
options: The date of the Easter festival only
The Catholic doctrine of two separate natures of Christ (divine and human) versus the EOC Tewahedo doctrine of one united divine-human nature
The practice of reading the Old Testament
questions.explanation: The Jesuits preached dyophysitism (two separate natures), clashing with the EOC's monophysite/tewahedo theology[cite: 375].

questions.question: Which document was authored by Emperor Galawdewos to defend the theological doctrines and liturgical practices of the EOC against Catholic criticisms?
questions.explanation: Emperor Galawdewos composed the 'Confession of Faith' defending indigenous Christian traditions[cite: 375].

questions.question: Under the diplomatic influence of Spanish Jesuit Pedro Paez, which Ethiopian emperor converted to Catholicism in 1612 and declared it the state religion in 1622?
questions.explanation: Emperor Susenyos publicly converted to Catholicism and decreed it the state religion in 1622[cite: 375].

questions.question: Which radical Spanish Jesuit Patriarch ordered the rebaptism of Ethiopians, re-consecration of clergy, and abolition of the Saturday Sabbath?
questions.explanation: Patriarch Alfonso Mendez introduced rigid, confrontational reforms that triggered countrywide civil war[cite: 375].

questions.question: What tragic event in June 1632 convinced Emperor Susenyos to abdicate the throne in favor of his son Fasiledes?
options: The bloody battle of Denqez, where thousands of peasant rebels were slaughtered by the royal army
A foreign naval invasion at Massawa
The loss of all crown jewels
questions.explanation: Shocked by the death of thousands of his Christian subjects at Denqez, Susenyos abdicated in 1632[cite: 375].

questions.question: What immediate political and religious measures were enacted by Emperor Fasiledes upon ascending the throne in 1632?
options: He embraced Protestantism and built new churches in Rome
He restored the Ethiopian Orthodox faith, expelled the Jesuits, punished Catholic converts, and instituted a 'closed-door policy'
He moved his capital permanently to Zeila
He surrendered the state to the Ottoman pasha
questions.explanation: Fasiledes restored the Orthodox church, expelled the Jesuits, and isolated the country from Europeans[cite: 375].

questions.question: What was the 'closed-door policy' pursued by the Ethiopian Christian monarchy after 1632?
options: A decree forbidding all trade caravans from moving at night
The strict diplomatic and geographic isolation of Ethiopia from European travelers for nearly a century and a half
The locking of church doors during Lent
The total ban on import of Indian textiles
questions.explanation: Fasiledes allied with Ottoman governors to block all European visitors, sealing the kingdom for ~150 years[cite: 375].

questions.question: What three theological factions divided the Ethiopian Orthodox Church following the Jesuit doctrinal controversies?
options: Tewahedo (Hulet Lidet), Qibat (Unction), and Sost Lidet (Ya Tsega Lij)
questions.explanation: Christological disputes split into Tewahedo (Tigray/Lasta), Qibat (Gojjam), and Sost Lidet (Gondar/Shewa)[cite: 375].

questions.question: Which historic church council, convened by Emperor Yohannes IV in 1878, officially declared Tewahedo as the sole orthodox doctrine of the EOC?
questions.explanation: The Council of Boru Meda in 1878 settled the prolonged theological dispute in favor of Tewahedo[cite: 375].

questions.question: What is the traditional, democratic governance institution of the Afar people called?
questions.explanation: The Afar organized their social affairs under an indigenous governance council known as makabanto[cite: 375].

questions.question: Which dynasty ruled the Awsa Sultanate in the middle Awash after its re-establishment around 1734 by Kedafo?
questions.explanation: Kedafo founded the Mudaito Dynasty, which used a silver baton as the prime symbol of sultanic authority[cite: 375].

questions.question: What is the traditional democratic council of the Somali people, where all adult males participate in collective decision-making?
questions.explanation: The Somali governed through clan and sub-clan assemblies known as the shir[cite: 375].

questions.question: Within the Somali shir council, what was the guurti?
options: The supreme council of elders mandated to resolve major inter-clan conflicts and crises
questions.explanation: The guurti was the esteemed council of elders responsible for arbitrating high-level disputes and social law[cite: 375].

questions.question: In the Oromo Gadaa system, how many years are in one Gadaa period, and how many Gadaa periods make up one generation (forty years)?
options: 4 years in a period; 10 periods in a generation
8 years in a period; 5 Gadaa periods in a generation
10 years in a period; 4 periods in a generation
12 years in a period; 3 periods in a generation
questions.explanation: A Gadaa cycle lasts 8 years; five sequential Gadaa periods make up one 40-year generational set[cite: 375].

questions.question: Which historic highland center served as the common gathering place where the Borana and Barentu confederacies instituted the Gadaa system c. 1450?
questions.explanation: Madda Walabu in southern Ethiopia served as the historic cradle of Gadaa reform and expansion[cite: 375].

questions.question: What Gadaa grade is entered by adult men aged 41 to 48 who assume political leadership of the Gadaa government?
questions.explanation: The Luba grade (ages 41–48) constitutes the governing executive administration of Gadaa society[cite: 375].

questions.question: What title was held by the elected leader and head of the Gadaa government during an eight-year period?
questions.explanation: The Abba Gadaa ('father of the period') serves as the executive leader of the Gadaa council[cite: 375].

questions.question: Which traditional institution was utilized by Oromo women to maintain solidarity and defend their customary social and legal rights?
questions.explanation: The Sinqe institution empowered women with spiritual and social authority to arbitrate conflicts and protect rights[cite: 375].

questions.question: Between 1522 and 1618, the Oromo population movement unfolded across how many successive eight-year Butta cycles?
questions.explanation: The northward expansion occurred under twelve successive eight-year Butta military cycles[cite: 375].

questions.question: Which Gadaa class initiated the first Butta wars (1522–1530), defeating the royal regiment Batra Amora and occupying Bale?
questions.explanation: The Melba generation (1522–1530) spearheaded the initial offensive, capturing Bale[cite: 375].

questions.question: Which Gadaa center served as the primary assembly site for the Tulama Oromo?
questions.explanation: Oda Nabee was the prominent political Gadaa assembly hub for the Tulama confederacy[cite: 375].

questions.question: What is the difference between Guddifacha and Moggasa in traditional Oromo social integration?
options: Guddifacha is the adoption of an individual child; Moggasa is the collective adoption and incorporation of an entire group/clan into an Oromo tribe
Guddifacha is a military oath; Moggasa is a grain tax
Moggasa applies only to cattle; Guddifacha applies to land
questions.explanation: Guddifacha is child fostering, while Moggasa is group adoption creating full tribal membership and mutual obligations[cite: 375].

questions.question: Which Oromo states in southwestern Ethiopia transitioned away from the Gadaa system to adopt monarchical dynastic rule (Moti)?
options: The Gibe Oromo states (e.g., Jimma, Limmu-Enarya, Gomma, Guma, Gera)
questions.explanation: The Gibe Oromo states evolved into centralized monarchies headed by kings (Moti) through contact with neighboring kingdoms[cite: 375].

questions.question: Who founded a new dynasty in the walled city of Harar in 1647 that governed the Emirate of Harar for more than two and a half centuries?
questions.explanation: Emir Ali ibn Da’ud established the independent dynasty that ruled Harar until the late 19th century[cite: 375].

questions.question: Who was the founder of the autonomous Kingdom of Shewa based in Menz in 1696?
questions.explanation: Negasi Kristos (r. 1696–1703) established the autonomous Shewan branch of the Solomonic line[cite: 375].

questions.question: Which Shewan ruler shifted his royal seat from Doqaqit to Ankober in the 18th century?
questions.explanation: Amaha Iyesus established the historic mountain capital of Ankober[cite: 375].

questions.question: What traditional systems of customary governance were maintained by the Sebat Bet Gurage and the Kistane respectively?
options: Yajoka Qicha (Sebat Bet) and Gordanna Sera (Kistane)
questions.explanation: The Sebat Bet governed via Yajoka Qicha, while the northern Kistane used the Gordanna Sera system[cite: 375].

questions.question: What is the generational age-grade system of the Sidama people, and what ethical moral code governs their judicial disputes?
options: Luwa (generation set) and Halale (the ultimate moral truth)
questions.explanation: Sidama society is structured into Luwa age-classes, guided by the moral principle of Halale[cite: 375].

questions.question: How did the Konso people transform their rugged, rocky terrain into fertile permanent agricultural land?
options: By clearing the hills with continuous slash-and-burn fires
Through sophisticated dry-stone terracing and specialized soil conservation techniques
By abandoning agriculture for deep gold mining
By flooding valleys with artificial canals from the Nile
questions.explanation: The Konso are renowned for stone terracing converting steep hillsides into productive farms[cite: 375].

questions.question: What title was held by the king of Wolayta, who rewarded loyal warriors with land grants?
questions.explanation: The king of Wolayta held the royal title Kawo, heading a structured administration[cite: 375].

questions.question: The divine monarch of the Yem kingdom, who acted as a high priest and governed with twelve advisors (Astessor), bore the title:
questions.explanation: The monarch of Yem was titled the Amno, reigning with attributes of sacred kingship[cite: 375].

questions.question: In the administrative organization of the Gamo people, what were the autonomous village units and the sacred communal assembly places called?
questions.explanation: The Gamo organized into autonomous political units (dere) that deliberated at communal grounds (dubusha)[cite: 375].

questions.question: What defensive fortifications were famously engineered by the Kingdom of Kafa to guard its borders against external invaders?
options: Deep defensive trenches and ditches called 'Erio'
Wooden watchtowers along the Red Sea
questions.explanation: Kafa protected its borders with an extensive network of deep trenches known as erio[cite: 375].

questions.question: Why did Emperor Fasiledes choose Gondar as the permanent royal capital of the empire in 1636?
options: It was located directly on the Red Sea shoreline
It overlooked trade routes connecting the Red Sea, Lake Tana, and Enarya, was shielded by mountains, and was free from lowland malaria
It had been the ancient capital of King Solomon
It was closest to the Ottoman garrison at Suakin
questions.explanation: Gondar commanded lucrative trade junctions, provided natural defense, and enjoyed a healthy plateau climate[cite: 375].

questions.question: Which emperor is considered the last powerful Gondarine monarch who restored state control from Massawa to Enarya before being assassinated in 1706?
questions.explanation: Iyasu I (Adyam Saggad) consolidated royal authority, introduced tax reforms, and asserted dominance before his death in 1706[cite: 375].

questions.question: Who was Etege Mentewab (Berhan Mogasa), and what role did she play in 18th-century Gondarine politics?
options: The Catholic wife of Susenyos who brought Mendez to Ethiopia
The influential empress from Qwara who dominated court politics, served as regent, and arranged political marriages with Wollo Oromo elites
A female general from Harar who conquered Semen
The founder of the Yejju dynasty
questions.explanation: Empress Mentewab steered Gondarine politics for decades as queen mother and patron of arts and architecture[cite: 375].

questions.question: What dramatic political event in 1769 initiated the Zemene-Mesafint (Era of Princes)?
options: The defeat of Ahmed Gragn at Woyna Dega
Ras Mikael Sehul of Tigray assassinated Emperor Iyoas and enthroned the elderly Yohannes II, establishing regional warlords as 'king-makers'
The expulsion of the Jesuits by Fasiledes
The crowning of Emperor Tewodros II
questions.explanation: Ras Mikael Sehul's deposition of Emperor Iyoas shattered imperial prestige, subordinating monarchs to warlords[cite: 375].

questions.question: Which regional dynasty, ruling from Debre Tabor, dominated the imperial throne in Gondar for seven decades during the Zemene-Mesafint?
questions.explanation: The Yejju dynasty (under Ras Gugsa, Ras Yimam, and Ras Marye) acted as dominant king-makers until defeated by Kasa Haylu in 1853[cite: 375].
